---
title: "Entanglement — Correlations You Cannot Explain Separately"
description: "A rigorous introductory lesson with one small example, mathematical notation and a proof-oriented explanation."
---

## Start with an ordinary situation

Two qubits are prepared together. When measured in the same computational basis, they always agree, yet each outcome is individually unpredictable.

## The core concept

Some joint quantum states cannot be factored into one state for each qubit. This is entanglement: a property of the combined system.

## Express it mathematically

$$
|\Phi^+\rangle=\frac{|00\rangle+|11\rangle}{\sqrt2}
$$

**Every symbol explained:** |Φ+⟩ is a two-qubit Bell state; |00⟩ means both measurements give 0; |11⟩ means both give 1; √2 normalises the two terms. The coefficients are probability amplitudes, not weights for a classical mixture.

**Substitute actual numbers:** The probability of 00 is 1/2 and of 11 is 1/2. The probability of 01 or 10 is zero in an ideal computational-basis measurement. The states are correlated, yet each individual qubit still looks equally likely to return 0 or 1.

## Why it works

Create this state by starting in |00⟩, applying H to the first qubit, then a controlled-NOT using the first as control. The second gate correlates basis states without measuring them.

## Go one level deeper

Correlations alone are not proof of quantum entanglement; classical systems can also have correlated outcomes. The distinction involves predictions across alternative measurement bases.

## Common misunderstanding

Entanglement cannot be used to send messages faster than light just by measuring one side.

## Check your understanding

Explain the example with different numbers. Identify which assumption makes the derivation work, and which assumption would invalidate it. Then write the mathematical model again without looking.
